title: Uddhava Gītā
alt_titles: Haṃsa Gītā (as a name for the whole, in some lists)
The last message of Śrī Kṛṣṇa

attribution.tradition: Kṛṣṇa's final teaching to his devotee Uddhava before leaving the world, recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and retold by Śuka
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (anonymous South Indian Vaiṣṇava composition)

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

structure.description: 23-24 chapters of the eleventh book (11.6 or 11.7 to 11.29); embeds the avadhūta's twenty-four teachers (11.7-9), the Haṃsa Gītā (11.13), the Bhikṣu Gītā (11.23) and the Aila Gītā (11.26)

summary: Kṛṣṇa instructs Uddhava to renounce attachment, see the world as the Lord's māyā and wander with equal vision. Through the story of Yadu and a young avadhūta brāhmaṇa it teaches learning from twenty-four teachers in nature, then expounds bondage and liberation, holy company, the guṇas, meditation on the Lord, the eighteen siddhis as obstacles, the three yogas of knowledge, action and devotion by disposition, the tattvas, worship (kriyā-yoga), and devotion as the easiest and highest path.

editions.name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Gita Press / critical ed. by H. G. Shastri, B. J. Institute, Ahmedabad)

notes: Chapter range varies by editor: some count the Uddhava Gītā from 11.6 (Uddhava's plea), others from 11.7 (start of the teaching). The avadhūta of 11.7-9 is named in the text only as 'an avadhūta brāhmaṇa'; the tradition identifies him with Dattātreya (cf. BhP 2.7.4, where Yadu and the Haihayas gain yogic powers from Datta). Eknāth's Marathi Eknāthī Bhāgavata is a celebrated commentary on this book.

title: Kapila Gītā

attribution.tradition: the avatāra Kapila, son of Kardama and Devahūti, teaches his mother; narrated by Maitreya to Vidura within the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; presents a theistic, devotional Sāṃkhya distinct from the classical Sāṃkhya Kārikā

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: Kapila teaches his mother Devahūti that the mind attached to the guṇas binds and turned to the Lord frees; that devotion without motive (animittā, ahaitukī bhakti) is greater than liberation itself; the twenty-four principles with time as the twenty-fifth; eight-limbed yoga culminating in meditation on the Lord's form; devotion graded by the guṇas; the misery of household attachment, death, the hells, the embryo's life and prayer in the womb, and the paths of smoke and light. Devahūti attains liberation.

editions.name: Kapilagītā with Hindi ṭīkā by Jvālāprasāda Miśra (Khemraj Shrikrishnadas, Bombay 1912), eBhāratī Sampat Ebharati-6675

notes: Circulated as an independent text (e.g. the 1912 Venkatesvara Press edition and the 1915 Gītāsaṅgraha, whose colophons read 'śrīmadbhāgavate kapilagītāyām'). Verses 3.28.37-38 recur verbatim at 11.13.36-37.

title: Haṃsa Gītā (Bhāgavata)

attribution.tradition: the Lord in the form of a swan (Haṃsa) answers the four Kumāras (Sanaka and his brothers) before Brahmā; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: Answers the Kumāras' question how the mind and the guṇas can be separated: the question 'who are you?' has no footing where the self is one; waking, dream and sleep are states of the intellect of which the self is the witness; abiding in the fourth (turya) the knower sees the world as the mind's play, like a whirling firebrand, and the body continues only while its karma lasts.

title: Bhikṣu Gītā

attribution.tradition: a miserly brāhmaṇa of Avantī who lost his wealth, became a mendicant and bore insults with fortitude; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: The mendicant's song: neither people, gods, the body, planets, karma nor time cause one's joy and sorrow; the mind alone turns the wheel of saṃsāra; all disciplines culminate in mastery of the mind, and the supreme yoga is its samādhi. It also lists fifteen evils rooted in wealth.

title: Aila Gītā

attribution.tradition: King Purūravas (Aila), son of Iḍā, after Urvaśī left him; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: Purūravas' lament of disenchantment after long infatuation with the celestial Urvaśī: desire is never sated, the body is a mere compound, association with the sensual must be abandoned; the chapter closes with the praise of holy company (saints cut the mind's attachment and are like a firm boat).

title: Rudra Gītā
location_in_parent: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.24 (Śiva's hymn/teaching to the Pracetās, c. 4.24.33-79)

attribution.tradition: Śiva (Rudra) instructs the ten Pracetās, sons of Prācīnabarhis, who are going to perform austerities; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: Śiva teaches the Pracetās a hymn to Vāsudeva and the path of devotion, declaring the devotee of Viṣṇu dear to him; the Pracetās recite it during their austerity in the water.

title: Gopī Gītā

attribution.tradition: the cowherd women of Vraja, when Kṛṣṇa disappeared during the rāsa; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: The gopīs' song of longing in separation (viraha) from Kṛṣṇa, one of the central devotional hymns of the Bhāgavata, much used in the Gauḍīya and Vallabha traditions.

title: Veṇu Gītā

attribution.tradition: the gopīs describing the effect of Kṛṣṇa's flute; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: The gopīs' song on the sound of Kṛṣṇa's flute and its effect on all beings of Vṛndāvana.

title: Yugala Gītā

attribution.tradition: the gopīs singing in pairs while Kṛṣṇa is away with the cows; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: The gopīs' paired verses remembering Kṛṣṇa's pastimes during the day's separation.

title: Bhramara Gītā

attribution.tradition: a gopī addressing a bee, when Uddhava came to Vraja as Kṛṣṇa's messenger; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: A gopī's reproachful song to a bee taken as Kṛṣṇa's messenger; Uddhava then praises the gopīs' love as the highest devotion.

title: Śruti Gītā

attribution.tradition: the personified Vedas praising the Lord at the time of creation (told by Nārāyaṇa to Nārada); recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: The Vedas' hymn on the Lord who is beyond all description; the chapter frames the question how scripture, which speaks through qualities, can describe the attributeless Brahman, and has been commented upon by Advaita and Vaiṣṇava schools alike.

title: Bhū Gītā (Bhāgavata)

attribution.tradition: the Earth, laughing at kings who strive to conquer her; recorded by Vyāsa in the Bhāgavata
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa and recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the opening of the Kali age (traditional reckoning from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (South India); some scholars allow earlier layers

summary: The Earth mocks kings who fight to possess her though they themselves are mortal; the passage teaches the vanity of conquest and possession.

title: Aṣṭāvakra Gītā

attribution.tradition: the teaching of the sage Aṣṭāvakra to King Janaka of Videha, with Janaka's responses
attribution.scholarly: author unknown; an independent Advaita text, not part of any Purāṇa or epic

tradition.text: the time of King Janaka of Videha (legendary)

scholarly.text: uncertain; proposals range widely (roughly the 8th to the 14th c. CE); most place it after Śaṅkara

structure.description: 20 chapters, 298 verses in the vulgate (1: 20, 2: 25, 3: 14, 4: 6, 5: 4, 6: 4, 7: 5, 8: 4, 9: 8, 10: 8, 11: 8, 12: 8, 13: 7, 14: 4, 15: 20, 16: 11, 17: 20, 18: 100, 19: 8, 20: 14). Some editions append a 6-verse 'saṅkhyākrama' listing the chapters and verse counts.

summary: Aṣṭāvakra answers Janaka's question how knowledge, liberation and dispassion are attained: you are not the elements or the body but the one witness, pure consciousness; rest in awareness and you are free now; bondage and freedom are only notions ('as one thinks, so one becomes'). Janaka voices his awakening (ch. 2 and ch. 6-20 in part), and the text describes the liberated one (18) who is beyond effort, meditation, duty and even the idea of liberation.

editions.name: Aṣṭāvakragītā with Hindi (Rai Bahadur Lala Baijnath ed.), eBhāratī Sampat

notes: Distinct from the 'Aṣṭāvakrīya' episode of the Mahābhārata (Āraṇyakaparvan 3.132-134; see src:astavakriya-mahabharata), where Aṣṭāvakra defeats Bandin at Janaka's court; the 1896 Pañcadaśagītā collection prints that epic episode as an 'Aṣṭāvakra Gītā' in three chapters. In recent times the text was loved by Vivekananda and read in Ramana Maharshi's circle (recent reception).

title: Avadhūta Gītā

attribution.tradition: sung by Dattātreya, the avadhūta; the closing verse (8.28) names 'Dattātreya the Avadhūta' as its maker; one colophon speaks of a dialogue of Svāmī and Kārttika, remembered as disciples who recorded it
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; date and provenance uncertain

tradition.text: sung by the avatāra Dattātreya (mythic time)

scholarly.text: uncertain; generally placed in the late first or early second millennium CE

structure.description: 8 chapters, c. 289 verses (1: 76, 2: 40, 3: 46, 4: 25, 5: 32, 6: 27, 7: 15, 8: 28 in the 1915 Gītāsaṅgraha edition)

summary: An ecstatic statement of non-duality from the standpoint of the realized: only by the Lord's grace does the inclination to non-duality arise; the self alone is, formless and all-pervading; there is no one to bow to, no bondage or liberation, no meditator and meditated. Chapter 8 defines the avadhūta syllable by syllable, repeats the Bhāgavata's list of the sage's virtues and warns the renunciant against sexual association and drink.
notes: Avadhūta Gītā 8.2-4 reproduce Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.11.29-31 (the qualities of the sage) almost verbatim. Chapter 8 differs in tone from 1-7; whether it is a later addition is not settled here (see REPORT).

title: Ṛbhu Gītā
location_in_parent: Śivarahasya, sixth part (aṃśa) (low confidence on the exact chapters)

attribution.tradition: Ṛbhu, a son of Brahmā and devotee of Śiva, teaches the non-dual truth he received from Śiva to his disciple Nidāgha
attribution.scholarly: part of the Śivarahasya, a large Śaiva 'itihāsa' of South Indian provenance; date uncertain

tradition.text: taught by Ṛbhu, son of Brahmā (mythic time)

scholarly.text: uncertain; late medieval proposals

structure.description: Sanskrit text of some two thousand verses in several dozen chapters (exact count not verified); a Tamil rendering (Ṛbhu Gītai) in 44 chapters exists

summary: Relentless statements that all is Brahman and that nothing else exists: the world, the jīva, mind, time, bondage and liberation are declared non-existent in the one consciousness; hearing and contemplating this teaching is itself presented as liberating, alongside Śaiva observances (sacred ash, rudrākṣa, worship of Śiva).
notes: The same teacher-disciple pair (Ṛbhu and Nidāgha) appears in Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15-16 (verified in the local e-text). Ramana Maharshi recommended the Ṛbhu Gītā and it was read in his presence (recent reception). Chapter structure and verse counts are not verified here.

title: Uttara Gītā
location_in_parent: claimed for the Aśvamedhikaparvan of the Mahābhārata (not in the critical edition)

attribution.tradition: Kṛṣṇa's teaching to Arjuna after the war, when Arjuna asked to hear again the knowledge of Brahman he had forgotten; a commentary attributed to Gauḍapāda exists
attribution.scholarly: a late independent Vedānta-yoga text attached to the epic; absent from the critical edition

tradition.text: after the Kurukṣetra war

scholarly.text: uncertain; late (medieval)

structure.description: 3 chapters (low confidence on verse count)

summary: Kṛṣṇa teaches Arjuna the knowledge of Brahman together with yogic anatomy (the nāḍīs, suṣumnā, brahmarandhra): the knower of Brahman, satisfied with the nectar of knowledge, has nothing more to do; the self is to be known beyond scripture, which is left behind like husk once the grain is taken.
notes: Distinct from the Anugītā (Mahābhārata 14.16-50), which is also a post-war teaching to Arjuna.

title: Jīvanmukta Gītā

attribution.tradition: attributed to Dattātreya
attribution.scholarly: short anonymous text; date unknown

summary: A short poem describing the marks of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), attributed to Dattātreya.
notes: Existence recalled, contents not verified; listed so that the hallucination sweep can confirm or mark it.

title: Īśvara Gītā
location_in_parent: Kūrma Purāṇa, Uparivibhāga (Uttarabhāga) 2.1-2.11 (colophons verified in the local e-text)

attribution.tradition: Śiva (Īśvara) teaches the assembled sages at Badarikāśrama in Nārāyaṇa's presence; narrated within the Kūrma Purāṇa told by Viṣṇu as the Tortoise
attribution.scholarly: a Śaiva-Pāśupata section of a Purāṇa whose frame is Vaiṣṇava; modelled on the Bhagavad Gītā

tradition.text: spoken by Īśvara in a former age

scholarly.text: c. 6th-9th c. CE (Pāśupata redaction of the Kūrma Purāṇa)

structure.description: 11 chapters of the Kūrma Purāṇa's second part: the secret knowledge of the Self (2), the unmanifest, time, pradhāna and puruṣa (3), the Lord's greatness (4-7) with Śiva's dance (5), knowledge (8), the Lord's cosmic form question (9), the liṅga as Brahman (10), yoga and the Pāśupata observance (11)

summary: Śiva teaches the Self as one pure consciousness distinct from body and mind, the Sāṃkhya categories under the Lord, his own supremacy (displayed in a cosmic dance), devotion and knowledge, and an eight-limbed yoga ending in the Pāśupata yoga of smearing with sacred ash and meditating on Īśāna as the supreme light, which frees the bound soul (paśu) from its bonds (pāśa).

editions.name: Kūrma Purāṇa, All-India Kashiraj Trust critical ed. (Varanasi 1971)

title: Vyāsa Gītā
location_in_parent: Kūrma Purāṇa, Uparivibhāga 2.12 onward (to c. 2.33, before the tīrtha section)

attribution.tradition: Vyāsa's teaching to the sages on the duties of the twice-born, following the Īśvara Gītā
attribution.scholarly: a dharmaśāstra-like section of the Kūrma Purāṇa

scholarly.text: with the Kūrma Purāṇa (c. 6th-9th c. CE)

summary: Vyāsa sets out the karma-yoga of brāhmaṇas: the student's conduct, study, the householder's daily rites, food rules, ancestral offerings, impurity, gifts, the forest-dweller and the renunciant, and expiations (chapter openings verified in the local e-text; the end point of the 'Gītā' is not).

title: Devī Gītā
location_in_parent: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.31-40 (7.31 the Goddess's appearance; teaching 7.32-40)

attribution.tradition: the Goddess (Bhuvaneśvarī) teaches Himālaya and the gods, as narrated by Vyāsa to Janamejaya
attribution.scholarly: modelled on the Bhagavad Gītā; a Śākta synthesis of Advaita Vedānta, yoga and tantric worship

tradition.text: spoken by the Goddess in a former age

scholarly.text: c. 11th-13th c. CE (with or somewhat after the Devī Bhāgavata)

structure.description: 10 chapters (DBhP 7.31-40); the 1915 Gītāsaṅgraha prints the teaching (7.32-40) as 9 chapters

summary: The Goddess declares herself the one consciousness, supreme Brahman, whose inseparable power is māyā; she shows her cosmic form, teaches that ignorance is the root of rebirth and knowledge its end, expounds eight-limbed and kuṇḍalinī yoga, meditation on herself as Brahman (with Muṇḍaka verses), three kinds of devotion by the guṇas and supreme devotion, her sacred seats and vows, and her external (Vedic and tantric) and internal worship.

editions.name: C. Mackenzie Brown, The Devī Gītā (SUNY 1998)

title: Bhagavatī Gītā
location_in_parent: Mahābhāgavata Upapurāṇa (chapters not verified; c. 15-19 recalled)

attribution.tradition: the Goddess (Pārvatī) teaches her father Himālaya
attribution.scholarly: part of the Bengali Śākta Mahābhāgavata Upapurāṇa

scholarly.text: with the Mahābhāgavata Upapurāṇa, c. 10th-11th c. CE (Bengal) (low)

summary: A Śākta Gītā in which the Goddess instructs Himālaya in knowledge, yoga and devotion to herself.
notes: Existence recalled with low confidence; contents not verified.

title: Śiva Gītā
location_in_parent: claimed for the Padma Purāṇa, 'uparibhāga' (Uttarakhaṇḍa), per its colophons

attribution.tradition: Śiva teaches Rāma (Rāghava) in the forest after Sītā's abduction, at the sage Agastya's prompting; part of the Padma Purāṇa
attribution.scholarly: an independent Śaiva Vedānta Gītā whose Padma Purāṇa attribution is not borne out by the printed Padma Purāṇa (low confidence)

tradition.text: Tretā age (Rāma's exile)

scholarly.text: uncertain; medieval

structure.description: 16 chapters (titles verified in the 1915 Gītāsaṅgraha): 1 excellence of devotion to Śiva, 2 dispassion, 3 the Virajā initiation, 4 Śiva's appearance, 5 boon to Rāma, 6 vibhūti, 7 the cosmic form, 8 origin of the body, 9 the nature of the body, 10 the nature of the jīva, 11 the jīva's course, 12 fruits of worship and knowledge, 13 liberation, 14 the five sheaths, 15 bhakti-yoga, 16 the qualified hearer

summary: Śiva, worshipped by Rāma, grants him weapons and teaches Śaiva devotion and Vedānta: the Virajā initiation with sacred ash, Śiva's glories and cosmic form, the formation of the body in the womb, the nature and course of the jīva after death, the five sheaths, liberation by knowledge of Śiva as the Self, and devotion as the means.

title: Gaṇeśa Gītā
location_in_parent: Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, Uttarakhaṇḍa (Krīḍākhaṇḍa), chs. 138-148 (chapter numbers low confidence; colophon 'gaṇeśapurāṇe uttarakhaṇḍe gajānana-vareṇya-saṃvāde' verified)

attribution.tradition: Gaṇeśa as Gajānana teaches King Vareṇya; told by Vyāsa to Sūta
attribution.scholarly: a Gāṇapatya adaptation of the Bhagavad Gītā (many verses reworked with Gaṇeśa as the supreme Lord)

scholarly.text: with the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, c. 12th-14th c. CE (Maharashtra)

structure.description: 11 chapters (verified titles): 1 the essence of Sāṃkhya, 2 karma-yoga, 3 exposition of knowledge, 4 prescribed renunciation, 5 praise of the practice of yoga, 6 buddhi-yoga, 7 upāsanā-yoga, 8 vision of the cosmic form, 9 discrimination of field, knower and known, 10 instruction, 11 discrimination of the three kinds of things

summary: Gajānana teaches Vareṇya the yoga that leads to liberation, redefining yoga as union with the supreme (not with wealth, kin, powers or heavens), and follows the Bhagavad Gītā's sequence of action, knowledge, renunciation, meditation, devotion, the cosmic form, the field and its knower, and the threefold classification by guṇas.

editions.name: Gaṇeśagītā with Nīlakaṇṭha's commentary, eBhāratī Sampat

attribution.tradition: commentary by Nīlakaṇṭha (Caturdhara), the Mahārāṣṭrian scholar best known for his Mahābhārata commentary
attribution.scholarly: 17th c. CE

scholarly.text: 17th c. CE

summary: A Sanskrit commentary on the Gaṇeśa Gītā reading it in the light of Vedānta.

title: Guru Gītā
location_in_parent: claimed for the Skanda Purāṇa, Uttarakhaṇḍa, as a dialogue of Umā and Maheśvara

attribution.tradition: Śiva's teaching to Pārvatī on Mount Kailāsa on the guru, told by Sūta to the sages
attribution.scholarly: a late devotional text in several recensions (c. 180 to over 350 verses); its place in the Skanda Purāṇa is not borne out by the standard printed editions (low)

tradition.text: spoken by Śiva on Kailāsa

scholarly.text: uncertain; late medieval

structure.description: recensions differ: the Ganeshpuri (Siddha Yoga) recension numbers 182 verses plus preliminary and closing verses; a Kashi 1920 edition prints about 230; three-chapter versions of about 350 verses exist

summary: Śiva teaches that the guru is Brahman itself: the syllable 'gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover; the guru is Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara and the supreme Brahman; the root of meditation is the guru's form, of worship his feet, of mantra his word, of liberation his grace. Without knowing the guru-principle, sacrifices, vows and pilgrimages are fruitless; the teaching is secret and to be given only to the devoted.

editions.name: Śrī Guru Gītā, Shree Gurudev Ashram, Ganeshpuri (sanskrit/raw_etexts digitization)
Gurugītā with Hindi, Bhārata Dharma Mahāmaṇḍala, Kashi 1920 (eBhāratī Sampat Ebharati-6674)

location_in_parent: Skanda Purāṇa, Sūta Saṃhitā, Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa, uparibhāga (colophon verified)

attribution.scholarly: an independent Advaitic Rāma text, probably composed c. 14th-15th c. CE, perhaps in Vārāṇasī in a Rāmānandī milieu; a major source for Tulsīdās

summary: Retells Rāma's story so that every episode teaches that Rāma is the supreme Brahman and Sītā his power, primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), who performs the events superimposed on him. It contains the Rāma-hṛdaya (1.1), Rāma's teaching to Lakṣmaṇa on māyā, knowledge and devotion (3.4), the nine means of devotion taught to Śabarī (3.10), many hymns, and the Rāma Gītā (7.5), and holds that devotion to Rāma is the means to knowledge and liberation.

editions.name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa with Hindi, Gita Press Gorakhpur (local digitization in sources_raw/raw_etexts/purANam/vaiShNavam/adhyAtma-rAmAyaNam)

title: Rāma-hṛdaya

title: Rāma Gītā

attribution.tradition: Rāma's teaching to Lakṣmaṇa, 'churned from the ocean of the Upaniṣads' (AR Māhātmya), narrated by Śiva to Pārvatī
attribution.scholarly: part of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; a compact Advaita manual

scholarly.text: with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, c. 14th-15th c. CE

structure.description: one sarga of 62 verses

summary: After one's duties have purified the mind, one should approach a true guru: ignorance is the root of rebirth and only knowledge removes it, not action, so knowledge cannot be combined with ritual action; the meaning of 'that thou art' is grasped by partial implication; the self is distinct from the three bodies and three states; superimposition is explained; one meditates on the Self, dissolves the syllables of Oṃ into it, lives out prārabdha free of ego and merges in Rāma. Until all is seen as Rāma, one should worship him.

title: Lakṣmaṇa Gītā

scholarly.text: late 16th c. CE

summary: No one gives another happiness or sorrow; each reaps his own deeds. Union and separation, friend and foe, birth and death, wealth and misfortune are snares of delusion; all this is like a dream in the night of delusion, from which yogins awake.

title: Vibhīṣaṇa Gītā

attribution.scholarly: Tulsīdās's composition

summary: The chariot that wins victory is dharma: courage and fortitude are its wheels, truth and virtue its banners, strength, discrimination, self-control and benevolence its horses yoked by forgiveness, compassion and equanimity, devotion to God its charioteer; one who has it can conquer even the invincible enemy, saṃsāra.

scholarly.text: the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya c. 10th c. CE (Slaje, c. 950); the Vedānta-oriented Yoga Vāsiṣṭha vulgate is a later revision (c. 11th-14th c.); older proposals ranged from the 6th to the 13th c.

structure.description: 6 prakaraṇas: Vairāgya (dispassion, 33 sargas), Mumukṣu-vyavahāra (conduct of the seeker, 20), Utpatti (origination, 122), Sthiti (persistence, 62), Upaśama (quiescence, 93), Nirvāṇa (liberation, pūrvārdha 128 + uttarārdha 216). The text names itself Mokṣopāya and claims 32,000 verses (2.17.6); the printed vulgate has roughly 27,000-29,000

summary: Vasiṣṭha teaches the despondent young Rāma that the world is a projection of mind within the one consciousness (cit), arising like a dream; that human effort (pauruṣa) guided by scripture and the good overrides fate, which is only past effort; that liberation comes by inquiry (vicāra) with the four gatekeepers (peace, inquiry, contentment, holy company), by the weakening of latent tendencies (vāsanā) and the stilling of mind and breath, through seven stages of knowledge to liberation while living. The teaching is carried by dozens of stories (Līlā, Karkaṭī, Lavaṇa, Śukra, Dāśūra, Prahlāda, Bali, Gādhi, Uddālaka, Suraghu, Vītahavya, Bhuśuṇḍa, Cūḍālā and Śikhidhvaja, the stone and others).

editions.name: Yogavāsiṣṭha with Ānandabodhendra's Tātparyaprakāśa (Nirṇaya Sāgara, Bombay 1911/1918)

notes: Book-level refs 1-5 in U06 teachings are checked against the Mokṣopāya critical edition, whose sarga numbering agrees with the vulgate for the passages used (e.g. the seven stages at 3.118, the gatekeepers at 2.11.59); Book 4 of the vulgate begins c. 18 sargas earlier than the MU's Book 4, and the vulgate splits Book 6 in two halves, so Book 4 and 6 teachings are anchored on src:moksopaya.

editions.name: Mokṣopāya, Historisch-kritische Gesamtausgabe (Krause-Stinner, Hanneder, Stephan, Krause, Slaje; Harrassowitz 2011-2019); GRETIL e-text (local: sources_raw/dcs/corpus/GRETIL/sa_mokSopAya.txt)

notes: Lineage placement is by reception only (the Vedāntic recension was absorbed by Advaita); the Halle editors regard the Mokṣopāya as neither Advaita nor Śaiva. It is scholarly metadata for the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha as well as a text in its own right; U06 anchors Book 4 and Book 6 teachings on it.
